A common path is: woodworking or mold apprenticeship/vocational school → learn drawing interpretation, cutting, and machine operation from an experienced craftsperson → start as a helper and develop manual and machine skills → learn CAD modeling and CNC programming → advance toward mold technician or workshop technical lead.

This work suits dexterous, patient people who can stay focused. It is a strong fit if you understand mechanical drawings, can spend a day amid sawdust and machine noise, and remain composed while measuring, trimming, and assembling.

Patternmakers, Wood create wooden casting patterns and core-box models from engineering drawings, preparing materials, laying out, machining, assembling, and finishing them. They are key manual and technical workers who turn designs into physical models ready for casting.

entries: Wood patternmakers create wooden casting patterns and core-box models from engineering drawings, preparing materials, laying out, machining, assembling, and finishing them. They are key manual and technical workers who turn designs into physical models ready for casting.
Prepare materials and lay out work from drawings, determining pattern structure and dimensions.
Machine wood manually and mechanically to create patterns, core boxes, and other components.
Assemble, glue, and finish patterns to ensure dimensional accuracy.
Support trial casting and correct patterns based on casting defects.
Maintain woodworking machines and tools and follow safe operating practices.
Record patternmaking process parameters and support process improvements.

paragraphs: Sawdust fills the workshop as you mark and cut materials from drawings. A pattern is rarely correct on the first attempt. After assembly, it goes through trial casting; shrinkage or deformation in the casting sends it back for correction. Revising one pattern three to five times is common. Overtime is routine for rush orders, and dimensional errors create even more rework, so no step can be rushed.

In short: turn mechanical drawings into wooden models that can be cast. Tasks include material preparation and layout, manual and machine processing, assembly and finishing, and repeated pattern corrections based on trial-casting results.

According to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS), about 500 wood patternmakers were employed in 2024. Employment is projected to fall to 400 by 2034, a net loss of about 100 jobs, with about 0 openings annually and a 2026 median annual salary of about $52,500 (BLS OOH, 2026).

AI will not immediately replace wood patternmakers, but it will change how the trade works. CAD modeling and CNC machining are taking over work from drawings to rough blanks, while 3D-printed sand molds are competing for simple patterns. The human core remains: manual assembly of complex patterns, corrections after trial casting, and customized pieces that machines cannot standardize. Traditional craftsmanship combined with new digital tools becomes more valuable.

paragraphs: A 5/10 means that about half of the desk-based and repetitive tasks in this occupation are becoming digital. AI and software assist with modeling, programming, and data management.

Moderate-to-high exposure does not mean high risk. AI takes over the standardized work from drawings to rough blanks, leaving customized correction, assembly, and trial-casting judgment. Simple patterns will become cheaper, while complex parts and correction craftsmanship become more valuable.

For this path, vocational school or CNC woodworking training is more suitable than purely theoretical education. Seek internships in foundries and mold factories, practice both drawing interpretation and manual work, and do not learn only machine operation.

Use CAD, CNC programming, and scanning measurement to advance from purely manual work to manual + digital work. Proactively take on complex prototypes and develop correction judgment, which AI cannot replace in the near term.

A woodworking background is best, but candidates without one can start as apprentices or helpers. In interviews, demonstrate that you understand drawings, describe parts you have corrected, and list machines you can operate.

Do not hire only machine operators. Versatile patternmakers who can correct patterns manually, read drawings, and learn digital tools will be scarce. Training must provide enough time for experienced craftspeople to mentor them.

This work suits people with steady hands, attention to detail, and tolerance for workshop noise. Shaping a pattern and producing a conforming casting from it provides a craftsperson's sense of achievement.

The pleasure of this trade lies in going from wood to metal. Your pattern is not decorative; it must be cast, measured, and revised to exact dimensions. People who enjoy hands-on work, have patience, and can turn drawings into real objects find the grounded satisfaction of craftsmanship here.

subject.summary: A wood patternmaker turns drawings into wooden molds capable of producing metal castings. Parts produced by a foundry often begin with the pattern in the craftsperson's hands.
